## How the forecast works {#how}

We forecast all 35 Senate races on 3 November 2026 by combining synthetic voter responses with polling information. We sample 100 personas per state from the 2024 Cooperative Election Study, giving respondents with larger survey weights a greater chance of selection. Each persona receives nine news paragraphs, and four language models answer its voting question three times in their own words. We score these answers using Semantic Similarity Rating (SSR), then average the scores to estimate each state's Republican share of the two-candidate vote.

The models' synthetic Republican vote shares are, on average, 5–9 percentage points higher than the polling estimates. We subtract each model's average difference from the polls to correct for this bias. This correction is based on polling estimates rather than actual election results. We then combine the adjusted model estimate with the state's polling average. For states without polling data, we instead use the 2024 CES vote share, adjusted by the average shift observed in states with polls. When combining the two estimates, we give less weight to the estimate with greater uncertainty, following the approach of Lock and Gelman [-@lockgelman2010], but our error estimates are approximate. We simulate 1,000 election outcomes for each model, allowing a shared national error to affect multiple states at the same time. We give all four models equal weight and include the 65 Senate seats that are not up for election to estimate each party's probability of controlling the Senate. In the [Discussion](#by-method), we compare this combined forecast with three alternative forecasting methods.

The forecast reports control of the Senate and the outcome of each of the 35 state races, using the latest news run and pooling all four models.

#### Battleground races {#battlegrounds}

Ballotpedia identifies these 12 races as battlegrounds [@ballotpedia2026]. Republicans hold nine of these seats; Democrats hold the other three, in Georgia, Michigan and New Hampshire. Our forecast may rate some of these races as less competitive than Ballotpedia's selection suggests.

Montana needs a qualification. Republican Kurt Alme faces both Independent Seth Bodnar and Democrat Alani Bankhead. Our two-candidate forecast compares Alme with Bodnar, the leading opponent in the polls, and leaves out Bankhead's share. It therefore does not capture the full three-way contest.

## Methods {#methods}

The voting responses are synthetic; we did not conduct a new survey. We used Python 3.12 [@python] with pandas [@mckinney2010], NumPy [@harris2020], pyarrow [@arrow], matplotlib [@hunter2007], requests [@requests], lxml [@lxml], tqdm [@tqdm] and python-dotenv [@dotenv]. Pilot embeddings used sentence-transformers [@reimers2019]. Tests use pytest [@pytest] and pandera [@bantilan2020], and the website was built with Quarto [@quarto].

### Data {#data}

Our personas were drawn from the 2024 Cooperative Election Study (CES), a survey of 60,000 US adults [@ces2024data; @ces2024guide]. Of these respondents, 38,307 lived in the 35 states holding Senate elections in 2026. Among them, 23,025 had a post-election voter-file weight, and 21,211 were validated as having voted in 2024. We used the post-election weight because the persona characteristics were taken from both survey waves. However, having this weight did not necessarily mean that a respondent had voted. We therefore applied the validated-voter restriction separately.

We obtained candidate lists from Wikipedia on 21 October [@wikipedia2026]. Each race pairs the Republican with the leading Democratic or Independent opponent. Where several names were listed for a side, we selected the candidate appearing most often in polls since 1 August. The opponents in Idaho, Nebraska and South Dakota are Independent. In Montana, Independent Seth Bodnar polls ahead of Democrat Alani Bankhead. The prompts acknowledge additional candidates without naming them individually.

Montana's candidate pair was corrected before the 31 October run. In the 27 and 29 October runs, Republican Kurt Alme was paired with Bankhead rather than Bodnar. As a result, both the synthetic responses and the matched polls referred to a different contest. The earlier Montana results therefore cannot be compared directly with the final run.

Polling data come from PollResults, which compiles Senate polls originally tracked by The New York Times [@pollresults2026]. We use them in the combined forecast and as a benchmark for the synthetic estimates. Polls estimate voter preferences; they are not election results. Their role in setting the weights is described below.

### Personas

Each persona describes a respondent's age, education, race, gender, household income, ideology and party identification. Age is measured in 2024 and grouped as 18–29, 30–44, 45–64 or 65+. Education ranges from less than high school to a postgraduate degree. Race has five categories: White, Black, Hispanic, Asian and Other. Gender distinguishes men, women, non-binary respondents and other responses. Income retains the survey's 16 brackets and its “Prefer not to say” option. Ideology ranges from very liberal to very conservative, while party identification distinguishes strong, weak and leaning partisans from Independents. Uncertain responses are retained as “Not sure.” The models do not see the respondent's reported 2024 presidential vote, which we reserve for descriptive comparisons.

### Weighted sampling

We draw 100 personas in each state with replacement, giving respondents with larger survey weights a greater chance of selection. Sampling with replacement allows us to use the same procedure in every state, including Wyoming and Alaska, where only 52 and 76 respondents are eligible. However, it also means that the same respondent can be selected more than once. Across the sample, 904 of the 3,500 personas repeat a respondent already selected in the same state. About two-thirds of selections in Alaska and Wyoming are repeats, so a sample of 100 personas does not contain 100 distinct people.

The survey weights are used when drawing respondents, rather than when aggregating their answers. Wang et al. [-@wang2015] used a different procedure: they adjusted an opt-in Xbox sample after collecting responses, using multilevel regression and post-stratification. In our procedure, the weighted draw reproduces each state's weighted CES composition in expectation. Each selected persona therefore counts equally within its state, and applying the survey weights again would double-weight the sample. This approach does not account for changes in the electorate between the 2024 presidential election and the 2026 midterms. Equal sample sizes allow us to forecast each race separately, but comparisons that pool demographic groups across states require state-level weights, as explained in [Crosstabs](#crosstabs).

### News summaries {#news}

We collect news from publisher RSS feeds, with Google News site searches as a fallback. Each collection covers the preceding 48 hours, removes duplicates and keeps up to 60 items per outlet. The collected titles, feed excerpts and URLs are saved in the repository (`data/01-raw_data/news/`). The ten outlets are The New York Times, The Washington Post, The Wall Street Journal, USA Today, Fox News, New York Post, The Daily Wire, HuffPost, Mother Jones and Vox. We group them as left-leaning outlets, newspapers and right-leaning outlets, following Pew Research Center's audience and political-leaning information [@pew2025sources]. “Newspapers” identifies a source group, not political neutrality.

GPT-4.1 Nano [@gpt41nano2025] screens titles and feed excerpts for US national significance and relevance to elections, policy, law or the economy. It then writes a short paragraph for each retained item. The instructions exclude sports and unrelated material and require a concrete development. Selected incorrect presidential and vice-presidential titles trigger a rewrite or exclusion. The paragraphs rely on titles and excerpts, not full articles, and the checks do not independently verify their claims.

Each persona receives nine paragraphs, with three selected at random from each source group. The selected paragraphs are joined without asking a model to summarise them again. We use the same news block for that persona across models and repeated queries, so these comparisons do not depend on different news selections. A fixed random seed reproduces the selection when the inputs remain unchanged, and retries use the saved dated selections. The following tables describe the retained news pool and show an actual persona block selected for illustration, rather than at random.

{{< include data/03-results/comparison/news_summary.md >}}

### Prompts and models

We ask each persona how it would vote in its state's Senate race and randomise the order of the two candidates. Models from four companies allow for systematic differences in their responses [@murray2026]. We record the returned model identifier and query time because a model can change while retaining its advertised name [@bisbee2024].

We use Claude Haiku 5.5 [@haiku2026], GPT-6 Luna [@luna2026], DeepSeek V4.1 Flash [@deepseek2026] and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite [@geminiflashlite2026] through OpenRouter [@openrouter2026]. Each model answers every persona's prompt three times. We score the responses separately and average their scores to reduce variation between individual answers. We request two or three sentences rather than percentages, leave generation temperature at the provider's default, and cap output at 800 tokens. Reasoning is disabled except for Gemini, which requires it and uses minimal effort. Empty, refused and otherwise invalid responses are recorded and excluded from scoring, rather than assigned zero support. Four Claude Haiku calls returned no answer in the 31 October run; calls and answers by model appear in the [cost table](#costs).

### Turning answers into voting probabilities {#scoring}

#### Why free-text answers?

LLM responses can concentrate on a small set of answers, a problem known as mode collapse. Heath and Alexander [-@heath2026] study whether free-text responses scored with Semantic Similarity Rating (SSR) better reproduce distributions in rating tasks. Maier et al. [-@maier2025] introduced SSR for purchase-intent ratings. We use this free-text approach for voting questions, without assuming that it prevents mode collapse.


#### Choosing the embedding model

On 26 October, we compared embedding models on 200 generated answers from Florida personas without news, 50 per voting model. Keyword rules identified 159 answers with a clear candidate choice. MiniLM placed 12 on the opposite side of the two-candidate scale; Gemini Embedding 2 misplaced one. MiniLM's errors involved answers supporting Nixon that also mentioned Moody. Adding both names to each anchor worsened performance, so we retained single-candidate anchors and selected Gemini Embedding 2.

The diagnostic was limited and did not validate scoring across all states. Neither setup captured indecision well. Answers expressing indecision received an average weight of 0.14 on the middle category, while leaning and definite statements often received similar scores. These results informed our choice of embedder, but they also show why the resulting SSR weights should not be treated as calibrated voting probabilities.


#### Semantic Similarity Rating

Gemini Embedding 2 [@geminiembedding2026] represents each answer and five candidate-specific statements as numerical vectors. The statements express definite support for the Democratic or Independent candidate, leaning toward that candidate, being undecided or choosing another option, leaning Republican, and definite Republican support. Cosine similarity compares the direction of the answer's vector with each statement's vector, producing five similarity scores per answer.

We rescale those five scores to the range zero to one and apply softmax with a temperature of 0.25. Adding the first two weights gives support for the Democratic or Independent candidate; adding the final two gives Republican support. The middle weight represents other choices, indecision or nonvoting. Answers and statements are embedded in the same way, without separate query and document settings.

These allocations are not calibrated probabilities of an individual's actual vote. Vote choice does not form an ordered rating scale, and the middle statement combines behaviours that may have different meanings. We do not apply a smoothing step or fit the temperature to voting outcomes, since these outcomes are not yet observed. Our procedure therefore differs from the rating applications in Heath and Alexander [-@heath2026]. Even when an answer clearly names one candidate, softmax may assign some weight to the other. This reflects how the answer is scored and does not mean that the personas' responses are more diverse.


### Combining synthetic votes with polls {#combining}

We draw on Lock and Gelman's [-@lockgelman2010] inverse-variance approach to combining forecasts and polls. They estimate predictive uncertainty from past elections. We adapt the weighting idea using approximate error scales for synthetic responses, rather than reproducing their full Bayesian model.

We first average each persona's scores over repeated answers. The state's Republican two-candidate share is the mean Republican score divided by the sum of the mean scores for the two candidates. Resampling personas 1,000 times estimates its bootstrap variability. The outside estimate uses information other than synthetic responses: a state polling average where available, or the weighted 2024 CES vote share plus the average shift in polled states (“2024 plus uniform swing”) otherwise. Polls must name both selected candidates and end within 45 days of the newest poll. We retain one question per poll, prefer likely-voter samples and weight two-candidate shares by sample size.

The combination is carried out in two steps. First, we subtract each model's average synthetic–poll gap across the polled states to obtain the corrected share $m^*$. This assumes that polls are correct on average across those states. It does not show that the original gap was necessarily a model error. Second, we combine $m^*$ with the outside estimate $t$ using $c=(1-w)m^*+wt$, where the outside weight is $w=V_m/(V_m+V_t)$. If the estimated synthetic variance is larger, the outside estimate receives more weight. The synthetic variance $V_m$ consists of the bootstrap variance and a structural variance. To estimate the structural component, we calculate the across-state variance of the differences between corrected synthetic shares and polling averages, then subtract the average bootstrap and polling variances. We apply a floor of $0.005^2$ to keep this component positive.

For polls, the error scale consists of sampling variance $p(1-p)/n$ and an assumed $0.03^2$ for error beyond sampling [@shirani-mehr2018]. In states without polls, it is estimated from the errors around 2024 plus uniform swing. We draw outcomes from a normal distribution centred on the combined share, with variance $1/(1/V_m+1/V_t)$. A shared national error with standard deviation 0.03 is then added. The correction assumes that each model's average synthetic–poll gap applies equally to every state, while the weights assume that synthetic and polling errors are independent. The resulting estimates are therefore approximate. The [Discussion](#by-method) compares this forecast with synthetic-only and no-LLM forecasts, as well as a version that retains the gap and includes it in the error estimate.

### Sources of uncertainty {#uncertainty}

The simulations include uncertainty from persona resampling, estimated structural synthetic error after correction, polls or the historical benchmark, and a national error shared across states. Pooling the four models also retains the differences between their forecasts. However, the average gap, variances and swing are estimated from the same polled states and then treated as fixed. Regional errors and dependence between synthetic and polling errors are not modelled separately. The [sensitivity analysis](#sensitivity) varies the assumed national and polling errors to examine how these choices affect Senate control.

### Tests

Before the full runs, we tested the workflow with five personas per state, free Laguna and Nemotron models, and a local MiniLM embedder. Separate pytest and pandera suites check the simulated data and actual runs. They test individual tables and consistency across the sample, answers, scores and forecasts.

The tests account for expected model–persona combinations and repeats, recorded failures, the returned provider and token usage. Missing or refused answers must remain missing after scoring. Valid scores must lie between zero and one and sum to one. Forecasts must assign valid vote shares and winners, fill all 100 Senate seats and keep the weighted estimate between its two inputs. Another check verifies that the combination uses the saved synthetic estimate and recorded weights.

To check whether the tests could detect errors, we introduced missing probabilities, probabilities summing to 1.3, invalid vote-share totals and answers from another provider into a copy of the earlier data. All of these errors were caught. Failed tests stop publication while preserving the paid answers. These checks assess whether the calculations are internally consistent; they do not assess the accuracy of the election forecast.

### Design

We used election coverage from CNN, Politico, NPR, CBC and Reuters as design references [@cnn2024; @politico2024; @npr2024; @cbc2024; @reuters2024]. The website and figures share a colour palette, typography and table style so readers can compare results without relearning the presentation.

### Sensitivity to the assumed errors {#sensitivity}

Our headline forecast assumes a national error with a standard deviation of 3 percentage points and an additional polling error with a standard deviation of 3 percentage points, beyond sampling error. The national component moves states together within each simulation. The polling component affects the uncertainty and weight assigned to polling estimates. These are modelling assumptions, not known error sizes. The table varies both settings to show how much the probability of Republican control depends on them.

## Evaluation {#evaluation}

The forecast cannot be scored against the actual results until after the election on 3 November. Therefore, we compare it with a prediction market that forecasts the same races using a different method.

### Against a prediction market {#markets}

This comparison follows Wang et al. [-@wang2015], who compared their Xbox-based election forecasts with prediction markets before election results were available. We use PredictIt [@predictit2026], which has a market for each of the 35 races and for control of the Senate. It provides another forecast to compare with, rather than ground truth, and combines information through trading [@rothschild2009].

For each news day, we use the daily closing prices returned by PredictIt's API, rather than a live quote. A winning contract pays one dollar, so its price roughly reflects a probability. We normalise the two selected contract prices so that they sum to one: the Republican probability is its closing price divided by the sum of both prices. Third candidates are excluded to match our two-candidate framework. Montana is excluded from the state comparisons on 27 and 29 October because the saved prompts used Bankhead rather than Bodnar (see [Data](#data)); the Senate control comparison retains the full forecast for each day.

{{< include data/03-results/comparison/markets.md >}}

Points on the dashed line are races where the two agree; points in the shaded corners are races where they favour different sides. Hollow points are races with an independent instead of a Democrat; states that differ by 8 points or more are named.](figures/latest/market_comparison.png){fig-alt="Scatter plot of 35 Senate races, our Republican winning probability against PredictIt's, with a 45-degree line and shaded corners where the two favour different sides." width="70%"}

## API costs and time {#costs}

Each run uses 3,500 personas. Four models answer for each persona three times, giving 42,000 calls per run. We calculate costs from the recorded token counts using OpenRouter’s list prices as of 25 October. Answer embeddings cost about US$0.50 per run, and news screening costs less than US$0.10. The total estimated cost is about US$9 per run. OpenRouter charged about US$7.20 per run because DeepSeek’s off-peak prices were lower. The total project bill was US$41.38, including the test run and a repeated run. The README lists the charges by day.

## Discussion {#discussion}

### Comparing four ways of building the forecast {#by-method}

The table compares four methods using the latest run's saved inputs. Synthetic-only uses the original SSR shares without polling adjustment. The combined forecast, used for the headline, subtracts each model's average gap from polls and combines the corrected shares with state polling averages. Where polls are unavailable, it uses the 2024 CES vote share shifted by the average change in polled states (“2024 plus uniform swing”). The third version combines raw synthetic shares with the outside estimates. Its error scale uses the mean squared synthetic–poll gap instead of the variance of the remaining differences after correction. Both the input shares and weights therefore change. The no-LLM benchmark uses the same polling averages and 2024-plus-swing estimates, excluding synthetic responses. The comparison shows how synthetic responses change the forecast, but cannot establish accuracy before election results are available.

::: {.firstcol-nowrap}
{{< include data/03-results/comparison/methods.md >}}
:::

::: {.chart-note}
The synthetic methods pool four models with equal weight. Seat intervals contain the middle 90% of simulated outcomes.
:::

{{< include data/03-results/comparison/method_summary.md >}}


### Do synthetic voters reproduce partisan voting patterns? {#fidelity}

Argyle et al. [-@argyle2023] define algorithmic fidelity as a model's ability to reproduce patterns of human responses across groups. We examine these patterns by comparing synthetic Republican support in the 2026 Senate races with the same personas' reported Republican vote in the 2024 presidential election. The comparison is made across demographic and party-identification groups, and the earlier vote was not included in the prompts. It therefore examines whether the models reproduce earlier partisan patterns, rather than whether they predict each person's next vote. Some Senate opponents are Independents, so non-Republican support does not always mean Democratic support. In the 31 October run, 54 per cent of all personas leaned Republican, compared with a 55 per cent Republican vote in 2024. Every gender, race, age, education and income group with at least 50 personas was within 6 points, except those without a high-school diploma (54 against 63 per cent).

Bisbee et al. [-@bisbee2024] caution that similar aggregate results can conceal overly uniform responses and distorted relationships between characteristics and opinions. The [Crosstabs table](#crosstabs) allows us to examine these differences by comparing synthetic Republican support with reported 2024 Republican voting across groups. Party-identification groups are useful for checking whether the models rely too heavily on party. Weak Republicans leaned Republican 97 per cent of the time, compared with a 92 per cent Republican vote in 2024; weak Democrats leaned Republican 5 against 13 per cent. The difference was greater among Independents, who leaned Republican 41 per cent of the time, compared with 61 per cent in 2024. Groups without a clear party preference therefore provide a harder check. However, agreement with the 2024 column would not by itself establish accuracy, since turnout, candidates and preferences can change between elections. In the polled states, the polls put the Democratic side about 6 points above its 2024 share, while the synthetic shares sit 5 to 9 points on the Republican side of the polls. We therefore use these tables to describe the synthetic sample, rather than to validate the forecast.

### Free text and Semantic Similarity Rating {#ssr-discussion}

SSR scores may not fully reflect the strength of support expressed in an answer [@heath2026; @maier2025]. Even when a response clearly chooses one candidate, the scoring rule can assign support to both. For example, strong Democrats leaned Republican in 1 per cent of cases, but their average Republican SSR share was 14 per cent. As a result, the scored group can appear less partisan even though the personas' answers have not become more diverse. Our limited embedding check also found that undecided answers were not clearly distinguished from candidate support. The final forecast is therefore affected by the reference statements and softmax temperature, as well as by the answers generated by the models.

### The news the personas read

Murray and Alexander [-@murray2026] find that including party identification in a persona can limit the effect of news on its answers. Our [news comparison](#synthetic) shows small changes in the average synthetic share across runs, although the changes differ between states. Since every prompt includes party identification, this may partly explain the stability of the responses. However, model answers also vary between runs. The observed changes therefore cannot be attributed entirely to news exposure, and they do not show that news has no effect on real voters.

### Uncertainty and the correlation between states

The [sensitivity table](#sensitivity) shows that the probability of Senate control depends on the assumed errors. If polls miss support for one party across the country, several closely matched races may change winners together [@gelman2020]. An error concentrated in one region could also affect neighbouring states in a way that our shared national error does not fully capture. Although the forecasts change little across the three days, their wide seat intervals still allow many outcomes. The stability of the forecast should therefore not be interpreted as evidence of accuracy.

### What agreement with the market tells us

Our forecast and PredictIt agree across many states in the [market comparison](#markets). However, a high correlation may largely reflect agreement in races where one candidate is strongly favoured. Differences in closely matched races matter more because a small number of seats may determine Senate control. In addition, traders can read the same polls used in our combined forecast. Agreement with the market therefore does not independently check the polling information. Low trading activity and the way traders value unlikely outcomes may also affect prices [@rothschild2009; @wang2015]. The comparison provides context, but election results are still needed to assess forecast accuracy.

### Limitations {#limitations}

Several limitations affect the interpretation of the forecast. First, we do not have results from past elections with which to estimate the typical error of this synthetic method. Unlike Lock and Gelman [-@lockgelman2010], we therefore use approximate error estimates rather than historical forecast performance. Polls provide a benchmark, but they may miss nonrespondents, misjudge turnout or become outdated as preferences change. If polls share an error, subtracting the average synthetic–poll gap may carry that error into the corrected synthetic estimates. The comparison without bias correction retains the gap and gives synthetic estimates less weight. As shown in the [method comparison](#by-method), both the input shares and the weighting rules affect the result. Neither version is known to be more accurate.

Second, the uncertainty estimates depend on assumptions. The estimated error sizes are treated as fixed, and not all dependencies are modelled, as described in [Sources of uncertainty](#uncertainty). This may result in seat intervals that are too narrow. The additional polling error has an assumed standard deviation of 3 percentage points, rather than a value established for these races; the sensitivity table also considers 2 and 4 points. Polls may also share errors even when they are collected through one aggregator [@shirani-mehr2018]. In addition, the bootstrap treats repeated selections of a CES respondent as separate personas. This may understate uncertainty, particularly in Alaska and Wyoming, where the respondent pools are small.

Third, the outside estimate in the 10 states without usable polls relies on the 2024 CES vote share plus uniform swing. Applying a common shift does not account for the appeal of individual Senate candidates. Synthetic estimates may also misrepresent how demographic characteristics and party identification relate to candidate choice. In Kentucky, for example, many personas identify as Democrats but describe themselves as conservative. Their synthetic responses should not be assumed to measure actual support for the Senate candidates.

The two-candidate framework introduces a further limitation. The final two-candidate shares do not fully represent other candidates, indecision or nonvoting. In Montana, Republican Kurt Alme is compared with Independent Seth Bodnar, while Democrat Alani Bankhead is omitted. As a result, the forecast cannot describe support across all three candidates or how the division of support affects the winner. Further scoring limitations are discussed under [Free text and Semantic Similarity Rating](#ssr-discussion).

Even when prompts are saved, provider defaults and model updates may change the answers obtained in a rerun. News was also collected on only three days, which limits what these runs can tell us about responses to other events. In future work, the amount and mix of news could be varied while the remaining inputs are held constant.

Some of these limitations could be examined with comparable forecasts from more elections. Such data would allow us to test the correction and weights, and assess whether error sizes differ by region or race competitiveness. They would also help determine whether models should receive different weights and whether estimating uncertainty across dates produces more reliable results.

### Conclusion: what the synthetic voters add {#conclusion}

Synthetic-only strongly favours Republican control, while the combined forecast and no-LLM benchmark favour the Democratic caucus. Including synthetic responses changes the result relative to the no-LLM benchmark, although they receive a small share of the combined weight. The project therefore illustrates how silicon sampling can be incorporated into an election forecast, without establishing that it improves on polling and historical information. Once election results are available, vote-share comparisons must use votes for the two selected candidates as the denominator, rather than votes for all candidates. Winner comparisons must also account for omitted candidates who could win or affect the outcome, especially in Montana. More elections and settings are needed to assess the method beyond these runs.
